params.title: Satellite Systems
params.subtitle: How a ship's Inmarsat-C, GPS, LRIT and Fleet Broadband equipment works, and how to track down common terminal and antenna faults.

onScreen: Inmarsat-C, GPS, LRIT and Fleet Broadband
How they work, and how to find faults
scenes.narration: At sea, a ship stays in touch through satellites. This lesson is about a GMDSS ship's satellite equipment. GMDSS is the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System: the international radio equipment and procedures ships use to call for help and receive safety warnings. We'll cover the Inmarsat-C terminal, the Global Positioning System, or GPS, Long Range Identification and Tracking, or LRIT, and Fleet Broadband. As the technician, you install, test and repair this equipment. By the end, you'll be able to follow a signal from ship to satellite to shore, explain how each system and its antenna works, and reason out the faults the exam describes. No background is needed: we'll start with how a ship talks through a satellite.

params.title: How a ship talks through a satellite

blocks.label: Satellite
blocks.note: A relay station high in the sky

onScreen: Satellite: a relay in the sky
scenes.narration: A ship's radio equipment for talking to a satellite is the terminal, and its antenna sends out and catches the radio waves. The terminal sends its signal up to a satellite: picture a relay station high in the sky, something that catches a radio message and passes it on. Any path up to a satellite is called an uplink. The satellite passes the signal back down toward shore, on a downlink. There, a Land Earth Station, or LES, picks it up with a large dish and passes it into the phone and data networks. Replies make the same trip the other way. Being so high, the satellite sees a huge piece of the Earth, so even a ship in mid-ocean can reach shore.

params.title: Inmarsat: satellites that stay put
items: Inmarsat: the satellite network GMDSS ships use
Satellites circle high above the equator once a day
They keep pace with the Earth's turning, so they seem to hang still
Each covers a huge area: an ocean region
Inmarsat-C for text messages, Fleet Broadband for calls and Internet

onScreen: Circle above the equator once a day
Inmarsat-C: text. Fleet Broadband: calls and Internet
scenes.narration: Which satellites does a GMDSS ship use? Inmarsat's. Inmarsat began as the International Maritime Satellite Organization, and its satellites orbit, or circle the Earth, high above the equator. The higher an orbit, the slower a satellite goes around. At that height, a lap takes 1 day, the same time the Earth takes to turn. So the satellite keeps pace with the spot below and seems to hang still in the sky. That's called a geostationary orbit, and it's why a ship's antenna finds the satellite in the same direction hour after hour. Each satellite covers a huge area called an ocean region. Of Inmarsat's services, 2 matter most here: Inmarsat-C for text messages, and Fleet Broadband for phone calls and Internet.

marks.label: 1530.0–1545.0 MHz
marks.note: Ship receives: downlink from the satellite

marks.label: 1626.5–1645.5 MHz
marks.note: Ship transmits: uplink, the higher band

onScreen: Transmit: 1626.5 to 1645.5 MHz, the higher band
scenes.narration: To reach those satellites, the terminal needs the right frequencies. A radio signal is a wave, vibrating back and forth; the number of vibrations each second is its frequency, counted in hertz. 1 megahertz is a million vibrations a second. Inmarsat works around 1500 to 1700 megahertz, in a range called the L-band. An Inmarsat-C ship terminal receives from the satellite on 1530.0 to 1545.0 megahertz. It can't transmit on those frequencies too: its own strong signal would drown out the faint one it's trying to hear. So it transmits on a separate band, 1626.5 to 1645.5 megahertz. The transmit band is the higher of the pair: receive low, transmit high. Exam choices swap or widen the bands, so learn these exact numbers.

params.title: Weak signals and noise
items: The satellite's signal arrives extremely weak
Noise: a random electrical hiss from every circuit
Amplifier: a circuit that makes a signal bigger
It boosts the noise too, and adds some of its own
Noise figure: how much noise a stage adds. Lower is better

onScreen: It adds noise of its own
scenes.narration: Now follow the signal coming down to the ship. After crossing tens of thousands of kilometers of space, it's spread out and extremely weak, like a flashlight beam that grows dim with distance. And it has company: noise, a random electrical hiss produced by every circuit, a bit like the chatter in a crowded room. To use the signal, the receiver must make it bigger, with an amplifier. But an amplifier boosts whatever it's given, noise included, and adds a little noise of its own. A receiver is a chain of stages, each a circuit with one job, such as amplifying. How much noise a stage adds is described by its noise figure. A lower noise figure is better.

params.title: The LNA: low noise amplifier
items: LNA: low noise amplifier
Not low noise antenna, not line noise amplifier
Receives and amplifies the very weak satellite signal
The first amplifier the signal meets
Sits at or near the antenna, not in the radio room

scenes.narration: That's where the LNA comes in. LNA stands for low noise amplifier: an amplifier built to add as little noise as possible. Not low noise antenna, and not line noise amplifier; the exam offers both. Its job is to receive and amplify the very weak signal from the satellite. It's the first amplifier the signal meets, the first stage of the chain. And it sits at or near the antenna, up on the mast, not down in the radio room with the rest of the receiver.

params.title: Why the LNA sits at the antenna

blocks.label: LNA at or near the antenna
blocks.note: Amplifies first, adds very little noise

blocks.label: Coax cable
blocks.note: Its losses come after the gain

blocks.label: Receiver
blocks.note: Noise figure set mostly by the LNA

onScreen: LNA at the antenna: amplifies first, little noise
Coax cable losses come after the gain
Receiver noise figure set by the LNA
scenes.narration: Why up on the mast? The weak signal meets the LNA first, right at the antenna. The LNA makes it strong while it's still clean, adding very little noise. Then the signal travels down a coax cable, a center wire inside a tube-shaped shield, to the receiver. The cable loses some of the signal on the way, and every later stage adds a little noise. But by then the signal is strong, so the losses and noise matter far less. Put the LNA after the cable instead, and the signal would arrive weakened, closer to the noise, and the amplifier would boost both together. Coming first, and adding so little noise, the LNA largely sets the receiver's overall noise figure, and lowers it rather than increasing it.

params.title: Signal to noise ratio
items: SNR: signal to noise ratio, also written S/N
Compares the level of the desired signal to the level of the noise
Not their distance, not their frequency
Higher SNR: a cleaner signal, easier to read

onScreen: SNR, or S/N: signal to noise ratio
Signal level compared to noise level
scenes.narration: The LNA keeps the signal well above the noise. How do we measure that? With the signal to noise ratio, abbreviated SNR, and sometimes written S slash N. It's a measure that compares the level of a desired signal to the level of background noise. Think of a voice in a noisy room. What matters isn't how far away the speaker stands, or how high the voice is pitched, but how loud it is compared with the chatter. Radio is the same. So the exam's wrong choices, which compare distance, or frequency, or a forward and a reverse direction, are out: SNR compares level with level. The higher the SNR, the more easily the receiver recovers the message.

params.title: Signal to noise ratio in decibels
steps: Signal power is 10 times the noise power
Decibels: each factor of 10 counts as 10 dB
params.answer: SNR of 10 dB: signal power 10 × noise power

onScreen: SNR of 10 dB: signal power 10 times noise power
scenes.narration: SNR is usually given in decibels, or dB. A decibel is a way of comparing 2 powers, or strengths, that keeps big ratios down to small, handy numbers. Let's work the exam's example: what does an SNR of 10 decibels mean? The formula: SNR is signal power divided by noise power. Suppose the signal power is 10 times the noise power. The ratio is 10 to 1. On the decibel scale, each factor of 10 in power counts as 10 decibels, so a ratio of 10 is 10 decibels. So an SNR of 10 decibels means the signal power is 10 times the noise power. That makes sense: positive decibels mean the signal is stronger than the noise.

params.title: Why signals fade
items: Fading: the signal weakens for a while, then recovers
Heavy rain soaks up some of the signal
Multipath: a copy bounces off the sea and partly cancels the direct signal
Too deep a fade, and the link drops out

onScreen: Multipath: a reflection off the sea partly cancels it
Too deep a fade: the link drops out
scenes.narration: Even a strong, clean signal doesn't stay perfectly steady. It fades: it weakens for a while, then recovers. Heavy rain is one cause: it soaks up some of the signal on its way down. Multipath is another: a copy of the signal bounces off the sea and reaches the antenna a moment later, slightly out of step with the direct one, so the 2 partly cancel. If a fade is deep enough, the signal drops below what the receiver needs, and the link fails. So how do designers plan for it?

params.title: Fade margin: signal kept in reserve

marks.label: Fade margin
marks.note: Extra signal to ride out fading

onScreen: Fade margin: extra signal in reserve
Normal level designed above the minimum
scenes.narration: With fade margin. Read the strip from the bottom up. At the bottom is the noise floor, the background hiss. Above it is the minimum usable level, the weakest signal the receiver can still read; below that line, the link fails. Next is the fade margin: a design allowance to accommodate expected fading. It's extra signal level built in above the minimum, like leaving early to allow for traffic. When a fade comes, the signal dips into that reserve but stays above the minimum. So the normal received level sits at the top, well clear of the minimum, and the link keeps working. On the exam, pick the design allowance; a ratio of largest to smallest values just describes variation.

onScreen: Ship's terminal sends the whole message
LES stores it, then forwards it
scenes.narration: Now meet the first system built on that technology: Inmarsat-C, the satellite text terminal most GMDSS ships carry. Inmarsat-C is a low-rate, store-and-forward data system. Low-rate means it sends data slowly, a little at a time, which is fine for text. Store-and-forward means each message travels as a whole. The terminal sends it up through the satellite to a Land Earth Station, which stores it, then forwards it to its destination. It's like posting a letter rather than making a phone call: the letter arrives complete, but there's no live conversation.

params.title: What Inmarsat-C can and cannot do
rows: Messages to and from a mobile unit
Broadcast data to groups of mobile terminals
Position reporting from fleets of mobile units
No: no voice of any kind

onScreen: Messages to and from a mobile unit: yes
scenes.narration: So what can a letter service do? Plenty, as long as it's text. Inmarsat-C provides message transmission to and from a mobile unit, which here means a ship's terminal. It provides broadcast data to groups of mobile terminals: one letter copied to many ships. And it provides position reporting from fleets of mobile units, each ship sending in where it is, so its owner can follow the whole fleet. What it can't do is hold a conversation. A conversation needs a live connection, open both ways at once, and a store-and-forward system never opens one. So Inmarsat-C cannot provide telephone communications via VoIP, Voice over Internet Protocol, which carries calls as Internet data, or any voice at all.

blocks.label: Ship terminals
blocks.note: Listen to the NCS when idle

onScreen: NCS: 1 per ocean region, per system
scenes.narration: Who directs all those messages in an ocean region? Each Inmarsat ocean region has just 1 NCS, a Network Coordination Station, for each Inmarsat system, such as Inmarsat-C. The NCS manages the region's channels, the separate frequencies the traffic travels on, a bit like a harbor master assigning berths. It sends out a common channel that idle terminals, those not busy with a message, keep listening to. The message traffic itself is handled by several LESs, the Land Earth Stations from earlier. With 1 coordinator per region, there's never any doubt about who assigns the channels. So remember: 1 NCS per ocean region per system, but several LESs. The exam offers 2, 3 or 4 NCSs. The answer is 1.

params.title: EGC: one message to many ships

onScreen: FleetNET: commercial messages to selected ships
scenes.narration: The NCS has one more job: it broadcasts EGC messages through the satellite. EGC stands for Enhanced Group Call: one message sent to many ships at once, like a radio announcement rather than a letter. EGC messages contain SafetyNET, FleetNET and System information. SafetyNET carries maritime safety information, such as navigational and weather warnings and distress relays. FleetNET carries commercial messages to selected groups of ships, for example a shipping company writing to its own fleet. And System messages carry network information from the Inmarsat system itself. Watch for near-miss names in the choices, like SafeNet or FleetwideNet, and for unrelated ones like grounding codes. The correct trio is SafetyNET, FleetNET and System.

blocks.label: Satellite
blocks.note: Up from the ship, down to the LES

onScreen: Up through the satellite to the LES
Back to the same terminal: whole path proven
scenes.narration: That's the network. Now the technician's side: how do you prove a terminal works from end to end? With a LOOP BACK test: send yourself a test message. First it goes up to the satellite, which shows your transmitter works. The satellite passes it to the LES, which sends it straight back, so the satellite and the LES work too. When your message arrives back at the same terminal, your receiver has done its part, and the whole path is proven. Asking the LES to send you a message would test only the receiving half. And pinging 127.0.0.1, a test signal to the address every computer uses to talk to itself, never leaves the computer, so it proves nothing about the satellite.

params.title: Voltage, current and a path
items: Voltage: the electrical pressure that pushes current
Current: the flow of electricity
Current flows only when it has a complete path
A worn wire touching an ungrounded case makes it live
Touch a live case, and you become the path

onScreen: A worn wire can make the case live
A person can become the path
scenes.narration: A working terminal also has to be a safe one, and that takes 2 ideas. Voltage is the electrical pressure that pushes electricity along, like water pressure in a pipe. Current is the flow itself, like the water moving. And current flows only when it has a complete path. Now picture a worn wire inside the terminal touching its metal case. If the case has no connection to ground, it now sits at a dangerous voltage. We call that live. The first person to touch it gives the current its path, straight through their body.

callouts.label: Terminal chassis connected to electrical ground
A fault sends current to ground: the fuse blows or the breaker trips
The case can't stay live
Never isolate the frame or insulate the supply from the hull

onScreen: Fault current blows a fuse or trips a breaker
scenes.narration: Here's the cure. To minimize shock hazard, make sure the chassis of the Inmarsat terminal, its metal frame and case, is connected to an electrical ground: a solid connection to the ship's hull. Now, if a wire touches the case, a large current rushes straight to ground. That blows a fuse or trips a breaker, the safety devices that cut the power when too much current flows. So the case can't stay live. The wrong choices, isolating the transceiver's metal frame or insulating the power supply from the hull, do the opposite: they leave the fault current no path except through a person.

params.title: Grounding the antenna to its mast

callouts.label: Never insulated from the mast
Antenna chassis grounded to the mast
Static and lightning energy find a path to the hull
Silicone weatherproofs the ground connection

onScreen: Antenna chassis grounded to the mast
Static and lightning go to the hull
scenes.narration: Up on the mast, the same thinking applies. An Inmarsat-C antenna should never be electrically insulated from its mounting mast. Instead, ground the antenna chassis to the mast. Then static electricity that builds up on the antenna, and the energy from a nearby lightning strike, have a path to the hull, instead of through the equipment and its cable. Weatherproof that connection with silicone, so salt spray can't corrode it. A corroded joint stops conducting, and the ground is lost.

params.title: Keeping water out of the antenna cable
items: Drip loop: a downward loop in the cable near the antenna
Rain drips off the bottom, not into the connector
Secured to the mast with a cable tie
Connectors sealed with sealant or putty, wrapped in self-bonding or vinyl tape
Not recommended: insulating the antenna from the mast

onScreen: Rain drips off, away from the connector
Never insulate the antenna from the mast
scenes.narration: Water is the other enemy. Form a drip loop in the transmission line, the antenna cable, near the antenna. It's a downward loop, so rain running along the cable drips off at the bottom instead of running into the connector. Secure it to the mast with a cable tie. Then seal the connectors with waterproof sealant or putty, and wrap them in self-bonding or vinyl tape. All of these are recommended practice. So when the exam asks which practice is not recommended, the answer is insulating the antenna from the mast.

params.title: A radio wave: 2 fields together
labels: Magnetic field, at right angles to it
Both travel together, out from the antenna

scenes.narration: That's how to connect and seal the antenna. But what kind of antenna is it? To answer that, we need 2 ideas, and the first is polarization. A radio wave, also called an RF signal, for radio frequency, is made of 2 invisible fields that vibrate together: an electric field and a magnetic field. A field is a push or pull that acts across empty space, like the pull around a magnet. The 2 fields stand at right angles to each other, and they travel along together, out from the antenna.

params.title: Polarization: the electric field's direction
rows: Turns as it travels, like a corkscrew

scenes.narration: The polarization of a satellite signal is the orientation of the RF signal's electric field component, not its magnetic field. It belongs to the wave itself, so choices that measure it against a dipole, a simple rod antenna, or against a dish are wrong. Picture shaking a rope: up and down makes a vertical wave, side to side a horizontal one. Those are vertical and horizontal polarization. In circular polarization, the electric field turns steadily as the wave travels, like a corkscrew. An antenna receives best when it matches the signal's polarization, and circular is the kind Inmarsat uses.

params.title: Radiation patterns
items: Radiation pattern: the shape of the area an antenna covers
Omni-directional: equal in every direction, like a bare bulb
Directional: one narrow direction, like a flashlight
Cardioid: heart-shaped, favoring one side

scenes.narration: The second idea is the radiation pattern: the shape of the area an antenna covers, sending or receiving. An omni-directional antenna works equally well in every direction around it, like a bare light bulb lighting a whole room. A directional antenna concentrates on one narrow direction, like a flashlight, and has to be pointed. In between is a cardioid pattern, heart-shaped, which favors one side. Hold on to the bulb and the flashlight; they come back later.

params.title: The Inmarsat-C antenna: RHC and omni
rows: Small, fixed, no motors to aim it
The ship turns and rolls beneath it
Sees the satellite on any heading
Matches Inmarsat's signal as the ship rolls
Would lose the satellite as the ship turns

onScreen: Omni: sees the satellite on any heading
RHC: steady as the ship rolls
scenes.narration: With those 2 ideas, we can describe the Inmarsat-C antenna. It is RHC polarized, meaning right-hand circular, with an omni-directional radiation pattern. Why this pair? The antenna is small and fixed, with no motors to aim it, while the ship turns and rolls beneath it. An omni pattern sees the satellite whichever way the ship is heading. And Inmarsat's signals are right-hand circular, so an antenna tilting as the ship rolls still matches the turning field, and reception stays steady. That rules out the wrong patterns: a cardioid or a highly directional one would lose the satellite as the ship turns. And it rules out the wrong polarizations, vertical or horizontal.

callouts.label: As high as practical
Free from shadowing by masts and funnels
Clear of other antennas and radar beams
No filter cutting above 1 GHz: that would block the signal

onScreen: No shadowing by masts or funnels
Clear of other antennas and radar beams
scenes.narration: Where on the ship should it go? Best practice is to install Inmarsat satellite antennas as high as practical, free from shadowing of structures such as masts and funnels. L-band signals travel in straight lines, like light, so a funnel between the antenna and the satellite casts a radio shadow. And far from the equator, the satellite sits low in the sky, where even a small obstruction can block it. Keep the antenna clear of other antennas and radar beams too, since their strong signals can swamp its sensitive receiver. That rules out mounting it right next to other Inmarsat antennas. And a filter that blocks frequencies above 1 gigahertz, which is 1000 megahertz, would block the Inmarsat signal itself.

params.title: GPS: satellites that tell you where you are
items: GPS: the Global Positioning System
Each satellite carries an extremely precise clock
It keeps broadcasting where it is and the exact time
Receive only: the ship never transmits back

onScreen: Broadcasts its position and the time
scenes.narration: So far, satellites have carried messages. Now a second family of satellites with a different job: telling the ship where it is. GPS, the Global Positioning System, is a set of satellites that broadcast timing signals. Each satellite carries an extremely precise clock, and keeps sending out where it is and exactly what time it is. Notice that the signal goes one way. GPS satellites only broadcast; the ship's receiver listens and never transmits anything back. That will matter for LRIT, coming up soon.

blocks.label: GPS satellites
blocks.note: Broadcast their position and the time

blocks.label: Travel time to distance
blocks.note: Radio travels at a known speed

blocks.label: Position fix
blocks.note: The one spot that fits every distance

onScreen: GPS satellites broadcast position and time
scenes.narration: How does a time signal give a position? The ship's GPS receiver notes when each signal arrives. Radio travels at a known speed, so the delay tells the receiver how far away that satellite is, just as counting the seconds between lightning and thunder tells you how far away a storm is. One distance only says you're somewhere at that distance from that satellite. Each extra satellite narrows it down, until only one spot fits every distance: the ship's position, called its fix.

How many satellites does this take? The usual GPS arrangement is 24 satellites, spread so that at least 4 are in view anywhere on Earth. They travel in 6 orbital planes, 4 satellites in each plane. An orbital plane is the flat ring a satellite's path traces around the Earth: picture 6 hoops, each carrying 4 satellites. The satellites orbit at 20,200 kilometers altitude. Unlike Inmarsat's, they don't hang still; they cross the sky, circling the Earth about twice a day. Each ring is tilted from the equator, and that tilt is called inclination: here, 55 degrees. The wrong choices mix in other numbers, so learn the set: 24 satellites, 6 planes, 4 per plane, 20,200 kilometers and 55 degrees.

params.title: Why at least 4 satellites?
items: At least 4 satellites for the highest accuracy
The receiver solves for 4 unknowns
Latitude, longitude and altitude
Plus its own clock error

onScreen: At least 4 satellites for the highest accuracy
scenes.narration: Why at least 4 in view? To provide the highest accuracy, a GPS receiver must receive at least 4 satellites. It has 4 unknowns to solve, and each satellite gives it one measurement, so 4 unknowns take at least 4 measurements. 3 of the unknowns are its position: latitude, how far north or south, longitude, how far east or west, and altitude, how high. The fourth is its own clock error. The satellites' clocks are extremely precise, but the receiver's is an ordinary one, and radio travels so fast that even a tiny timing error throws every distance off. So the receiver treats its clock error as one more unknown. The answer is 4, not 2, 6 or 8.

marks.label: L1: 1575.42 MHz
marks.note: Navigation message and SPS code signals

onScreen: L1: 1575.42 MHz, navigation message and SPS code
scenes.narration: What exactly do the satellites send? Each transmits 2 carriers. A carrier is the steady radio wave the information rides on, the way a truck carries its load. Lower on the strip is L2, at 1227.60 megahertz, used to measure the ionospheric delay; more on that next. Higher is L1, at 1575.42 megahertz. It carries the navigation message, which tells the receiver where each satellite is and the time, and the SPS code signals. SPS stands for Standard Positioning Service: the service everyday civilian receivers use. The 2 carriers are transmitted separately, not combined in a mixer, a circuit that blends signals together. And 1650.5 megahertz, a common trap, is not a GPS frequency at all.

params.title: L2 and the ionospheric delay
items: Ionosphere: a layer of electrically charged air high above the Earth
It slows GPS signals slightly: the ionospheric delay
The delay depends on frequency
Compare L1 and L2 arrival times to remove it
L2, 1227.60 MHz: measures the ionospheric delay

onScreen: Compare L1 and L2 to remove it
scenes.narration: Now that delay. High above the weather lies the ionosphere, a layer of air that sunlight has electrically charged. GPS signals pass through it on their way down, and it slows them slightly. That's the ionospheric delay, and it makes each satellite seem a little farther away than it is. Here's the trick: the delay depends on frequency, and lower frequencies are slowed more. So a dual-frequency receiver compares the arrival times on L1 and L2, works out the delay and removes it. That's why the L2 carrier of 1227.60 megahertz is used to measure the ionospheric delay. The traps pin the wrong numbers on L1 and L2, so pair them carefully: L1, 1575.42, navigation message; L2, 1227.60, ionospheric delay.

blocks.label: DGPS reference station
blocks.note: Fixed, at a precisely surveyed point

onScreen: Reference station at a surveyed point
scenes.narration: Even after that, small errors remain. Differential GPS, or DGPS, cleans most of them up. It corrects for various errors using a fixed receiving station at a precisely surveyed point. The station knows exactly where it is, so it compares that with what GPS tells it. The difference is the error, and ships nearby see almost the same error. So the station transmits corrections via radio signals. Marine systems use MF, medium frequency, radiobeacons in the 285 to 325 kilohertz band. A kilohertz is 1000 vibrations a second, far below GPS frequencies. The ship's GPS receiver applies the corrections. The traps send corrections inside the GPS signal itself, or compare L1 and L2. DGPS uses its own radio link.

params.title: Sharing GPS data on the bridge

scenes.narration: With a corrected position in hand, the GPS shares it around the bridge. GPS is usually interconnected with other bridge equipment through a NMEA 0183 or NMEA 2000 LAN. NMEA is the National Marine Electronics Association, which sets the standards, and a LAN, a local area network, is wiring that lets nearby equipment share data. Over it, the GPS sends position, speed and time to the radars; to the DSC radios, DSC being digital selective calling, the automatic calling built into GMDSS radios; to ECDIS, the electronic chart display and information system; and to the autopilots. The traps offer an ordinary Ethernet LAN, a USB port or a parallel line. For the exam, it's NMEA 0183 or NMEA 2000.

params.title: LRIT: tracking for the flag state
items: LRIT: Long Range Identification and Tracking
Flag state: the country a ship is registered in
Identity, position and time go to a data center
Then on to the ship's own flag administration
A separate tracking system for each flag state's security

onScreen: LRIT: Long Range Identification and Tracking
Flag state: where the ship is registered
Separate system for each flag state's security
scenes.narration: Now we can put 2 ideas together: a position from GPS, sent as a message over Inmarsat-C. That's LRIT, Long Range Identification and Tracking. The exam also calls it Long Range Identity Tracking or Long Range Information Tracking. Every ship is registered in a country, its flag state, whose flag it flies. The ship's identity, position and time go through a data center to its own flag administration, the government office in charge of that country's ships. So LRIT data is a separate tracking system for each flag state's security.

params.title: LRIT is not AIS or AMVER
rows: VHF broadcast to all ships nearby
Not on AIS channels, not a backup

onScreen: LRIT not broadcast on the Internet
scenes.narration: The exam's wrong answers mix LRIT up with 2 other systems. AIS, the Automatic Identification System, has every ship broadcast its identity and position by VHF, very high frequency, radio to everyone nearby. LRIT doesn't use AIS channels, and it isn't a backup for AIS. AMVER, the Automated Mutual-assistance Vessel Rescue system, is a voluntary reporting system that helps rescuers find ships near an emergency. Sending AMVER reports doesn't replace LRIT. And LRIT is not broadcast on the Internet for company tracking. It's a separate, private system.

blocks.label: Inmarsat-C satellite
blocks.note: LRIT is detected on this network

blocks.label: LRIT data center
blocks.note: For US ships: the National Data Center

onScreen: GPS: broadcasts only, supplies the position
Inmarsat-C or Mini-C terminal sends the report
Inmarsat-D+ or Iridium can also carry it
Data center, then the flag administration
scenes.narration: How does a report get there? GPS supplies the ship's position. But GPS does not support LRIT: its satellites only broadcast, and can't carry a report back. The report goes out from the GMDSS Inmarsat-C or Mini-C terminal, Mini-C being a smaller version of the same terminal. That's how most ships meet the requirement, so LRIT is detected on the Inmarsat-C satellite network. Inmarsat-D plus or Iridium, other 2-way satellite systems, can also carry it. From the satellite, the report reaches the data center, then the flag administration. So when the exam asks which satellite system does not support LRIT, the answer is GPS.

badges.label: APR: automatic position report
badges.note: Sent automatically, no one pressing a button

badges.label: Hours in a day, divided by 6
U.S. National Data Center
badges.note: Position reports from each US Flag ship

onScreen: At least 4 reports a day to the National Data Center
scenes.narration: How often does the ship report? An LRIT terminal must be capable of being configured to automatically transmit an APR, an automatic position report: it sends one on its own, with no one pressing a button. It must transmit an APR every 6 hours. A day has 24 hours, and 24 divided by 6 is 4, so that's 4 reports a day. That's why the U.S. National Data Center must receive at least 4 position reports daily from each US Flag ship. The traps say every 12, 8 or 24 hours, or every hour.

params.title: Poll and PR: a report on request

blocks.label: LRIT data center
blocks.note: Sends a poll: a request for a report

scenes.narration: The data center can also ask for a report whenever it wants one. That request is called a poll, and it's what the exam means when it says the National Data Center monitors polling input for each US Flag ship. The poll goes out to the ship's LRIT terminal. The terminal must be able to automatically transmit a PR, a position report, if requested by a poll. So the PR goes straight back, again with no one aboard pressing a button. Watch for a trap that has the terminal receive an APR instead of sending one. And the number of crew aboard is not part of any report.

params.title: LRIT not reporting? Check the right unit
rows: No: AIS plays no part in LRIT

onScreen: Check the GMDSS console's Inmarsat-C terminal
Not the Ship Security Alert System
scenes.narration: And if the reports stop? Suppose a compulsory equipped IMO ship, one the International Maritime Organization's rules require to carry LRIT, is not correctly broadcasting its LRIT information. What should you do? Double check the GMDSS console's Inmarsat-C terminal for regular operation, because that terminal is what sends the reports. Rebooting the AIS unit won't help: AIS plays no part in LRIT. And the Ship Security Alert System is a different system altogether. So at the terminal, check 3 things. Is it powered? Is it logged in, meaning signed on to the satellite network, the way a mobile phone registers with its network? And is it working normally?

params.title: Fleet Broadband: calls and Internet
items: Inmarsat-C: slow text messages, small fixed antenna
Fleet Broadband: phone calls and fast data
The maritime form of BGAN: Broadband Global Area Network
Older family: Fleet 77, Fleet 55 and Fleet 33
Needs an antenna that keeps pointing at the satellite

onScreen: Fleet Broadband: calls and fast data
scenes.narration: That completes Inmarsat-C's jobs: messages, safety broadcasts and LRIT reports. But Inmarsat-C handles text, slowly. For phone calls and Internet, ships use Fleet Broadband, the maritime form of Inmarsat's BGAN service. BGAN stands for Broadband Global Area Network, and broadband simply means a fast data connection. Before Fleet Broadband came an older family of Inmarsat ship terminals, Fleet 77, Fleet 55 and Fleet 33, and the exam still asks about them. All of them move far more data than Inmarsat-C, and fast data needs a stronger signal. So instead of a small antenna that hears equally in every direction, they use a directional antenna that concentrates on the satellite and keeps pointing at it as the ship turns and rolls.

params.title: Fleet Broadband: above and below deck

callouts.label: Radome above deck: antenna, RF and antenna-control electronics
Below deck: the Fleet Broadband terminal
The terminal stores the configuration data
It contains all user interfaces and LED indicators
Not a Main Control Unit or Master Communications Unit

onScreen: Radome above deck: antenna, RF and antenna-control electronics
Below deck: the Fleet Broadband terminal
All user interfaces and LED indicators
Not a Main Control Unit or Master Communications Unit
scenes.narration: Let's look at the hardware. A Fleet Broadband installation comes in 2 parts. Above deck sits the radome, a weatherproof dome over the antenna. It holds the antenna, the RF electronics that transmit and receive, and the antenna-control electronics that keep it aimed. Below deck is the Fleet Broadband terminal, a component of the below deck equipment. It stores the configuration data, meaning all its settings, and it contains all the user interfaces, the sockets and controls you connect to, and the LED indicators: the small status lights, LED meaning light-emitting diode. So the unit with the configuration data, interfaces and LEDs is the Fleet Broadband terminal. Trap names like Main Control Unit or Master Communications Unit are not the answer.

params.title: Inside a Fleet Broadband radome
items: Stabilized antenna
RF unit
Antenna Control Unit (ACU)
GPS antenna
Not: rotary joint, gyro-stabilized platform, high voltage supply

onScreen: Not a rotary joint, gyro platform or high voltage supply
scenes.narration: Let's open the radome. An Inmarsat Fleet Broadband radome typically includes 4 parts. First, a stabilized antenna: motors hold it steady and on target while the ship rolls and turns. Second, an RF unit, which transmits and receives. Third, an Antenna Control Unit, or ACU, which works out where to point and drives the antenna there. And fourth, a GPS antenna, because the system needs to know where the ship is to know where in the sky the satellite is. Learn the 4 together: stabilized antenna, RF unit, ACU and GPS antenna. The wrong choices swap in other parts, such as a rotary joint, a gyro-stabilized platform or a high voltage power supply.

params.title: Omni-directional or directional?
rows: A narrow beam, like a flashlight

onScreen: Omni: every direction. Directional: a narrow beam
scenes.narration: That stabilized antenna is directional. Remember the bulb and the flashlight? Inmarsat-C's omni-directional antenna is the bulb, covering every direction, but thinly. A directional antenna is the flashlight, squeezing its energy into a narrow beam. How much stronger the signal is in that favored direction is called gain: low for the bulb, high for the flashlight. It works the same way when receiving: a directional antenna collects far more from the direction it faces. The narrower the beam, the higher the gain. The price is aiming. An omni antenna needs none, but a directional one must point at the satellite. That's why Inmarsat-C gets by with a fixed omni antenna, while Fleet Broadband's is directional and stabilized.

params.title: The parabolic dish
items: Curved reflector focuses energy onto the focal point
Feedhorn adjusted to the focal point, not behind the reflector
High gain, narrow beam
Suits microwaves like the L-band, not HF (3-30 MHz)

onScreen: Reflector focuses onto the focal point
scenes.narration: The classic directional antenna is the parabolic dish. Its curved reflector focuses incoming energy onto a single spot in front of it, the focal point, the way a curved mirror can focus sunlight. So the feedhorn, the small pickup that collects that energy, is adjusted to the focal point of the antenna. Not behind the reflector, where no energy arrives. Dishes give high gain and narrow beams, so a choice calling them low gain is wrong. And they suit microwave frequencies, the range the L-band belongs to, not HF, high frequency, 3 to 30 megahertz, where the waves are so long a dish would have to be enormous.

params.title: Phase: in step or out of step
labels: Phase: where a wave is in its swing
In step: the waves add up
Out of step: the waves cancel

onScreen: Phase: where a wave is in its swing
scenes.narration: A dish must be physically turned to aim it. There's another way to aim a beam, with nothing moving, and it rests on one idea: phase. Phase is the timing of a wave: where it is in its up-and-down swing at a given moment. When 2 waves meet in step, peak with peak, they add up into a bigger wave, like 2 people pushing a swing together: it goes higher. When they meet out of step, the peak of one with the low point of the other, they cancel, like 2 people pushing against each other: the swing barely moves.

A phased array uses that idea. The RF is shared out to a set of phase shifters, circuits that each delay the wave by a chosen amount. Each shifter feeds one of multiple small antenna elements, fixed side by side. In one direction, the waves from the elements arrive in step and add into a strong beam; elsewhere, they cancel. So in a phased array antenna system, the RF from multiple antennas is varied in phase, and often in amplitude, meaning strength, to produce a desired radiation pattern. Change the phases, and the beam steers electronically. The wrong choices have a single element doing all the work, or the antennas combined for unity gain, meaning no gain at all.

params.title: Protocols at the LAN port
rows: The basic rules of network data

onScreen: TCP/IP: what a PC on the LAN port uses
SMTP and FTP ride on top of TCP/IP
scenes.narration: That's the antenna side. Now back below deck, to the terminal's sockets. The most important is the LAN port, also called the Ethernet port: the same socket home and office networks use. To talk over it, devices follow a protocol, an agreed set of rules for exchanging data, like a shared language. A PC connected to the LAN interface of an Inmarsat terminal uses the TCP IP protocol: Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol, the basic language of the Internet. The exam also lists SMTP, for e-mail, and FTP, for file transfer. Those ride on top of TCP IP, so they aren't the answer. And ISDN, the Integrated Services Digital Network, is a digital telephone standard with its own port.

onScreen: ISDN handset: its own ISDN port
scenes.narration: What does the LAN port connect? On a Fleet Broadband terminal, the LAN, or Ethernet, port provides IP connectivity, meaning a network link that speaks Internet Protocol, for 3 things. Terminal configuration and troubleshooting from a computer, through the terminal's built-in web pages. Internet browsing with a computer. And a Voice over IP telephone handset. Connecting an ISDN telephone handset is not a function of the LAN port. An ISDN handset speaks ISDN, not IP, so it plugs into the terminal's dedicated ISDN port. When the exam asks which is NOT a LAN port function, pick the ISDN handset.

Take a closer look at that Voice over IP handset. It's the Fleet Broadband IP handset: a telephone that plugs into the LAN port. It makes Voice over IP telephone calls, and it uses TCP IP to communicate with the terminal. Over the satellite, its calls can be transmitted as circuit-switched calls, meaning a dedicated connection held open for the whole call, like a traditional phone line. Through its menus, it can display terminal status and change terminal parameters, the terminal's settings. What it doesn't do is polling and data reporting. That's an Inmarsat-C function: remember the LRIT polls and position reports. So it's the odd one out when the exam lists the handset's functions.

blocks.label: Terminal
blocks.note: Gets no power from the handset

onScreen: PoE: power over the network cable
From the terminal's LAN port to the handset
Never from the handset to the terminal
scenes.narration: One more handset fact catches people out: power. The handset gets its electricity through its network cable. That's called Power over Ethernet, or PoE: power sent down the same cable as the data, so no separate power cord is needed. But which way does it flow? From the terminal's LAN port to the handset. The handset does not provide the terminal with Power over Ethernet; a small handset couldn't run the terminal. So among the handset's characteristics, providing the terminal with Power over Ethernet is the one that's false.

params.title: RJ11 ports: standard voice
items: RJ11: the ordinary small telephone socket
RJ11 Port 1 and 2: standard voice or 3.1 kHz audio
Standard voice: compressed speech, costs less
F500 phones: set RJ11 Port 1 and 2 to standard voice

onScreen: Port 1 and 2: standard voice or 3.1 kHz audio
scenes.narration: Besides its LAN ports, the terminal has RJ11 ports: the ordinary telephone sockets that plain phones and fax machines plug into. On Thrane and Thrane F250 and F500 terminals, Thrane and Thrane being the maker, RJ11 Port 1 and 2 can be set 2 ways: standard voice, or 3.1 kilohertz audio. Standard voice is a compressed speech service. A codec, a circuit that squeezes sound into fewer bits, the 1s and 0s of digital data, keeps what makes speech understandable and drops the rest. That uses less satellite capacity, so standard voice costs less. For standard voice telephone operation on the F500, set RJ11 Port 1 and 2 to standard voice. Not 3.1 kilohertz, and not the ISDN port.

params.title: Fax needs 3.1 kHz audio
rows: RJ11 Port 1 and 2 set to this

onScreen: 3.1 kHz audio: fax machines and modems
A speech codec garbles fax tones; 3.1 kHz audio passes them clean
Fax and Data: RJ11 Port 1 and 2 on 3.1 kHz audio
scenes.narration: So ordinary phones go on standard voice. Fax machines and modems are different. A modem is a device that sends computer data as sound. Both send their data as tones, and a speech codec garbles those tones, because it was built only to keep speech understandable. The 3.1 kilohertz audio setting passes the whole ordinary telephone sound band, about 3.1 kilohertz wide, through unprocessed. So the correct Fax and Data configuration of a Fleet Broadband terminal is RJ11 Port 1 and 2 set to 3.1 kilohertz audio. Not standard voice, which would garble the tones. Not the ISDN port. And not the LAN ports, which carry IP data, not audio.

params.title: F250 and F500 fax: Group 3
items: Thrane & Thrane F250 and F500 terminals
Fax: Group 3 fax via the 3.1 kHz audio channel
Group 3: the standard for ordinary analog fax machines
Not via standard voice, not via ISDN
No Group 5 fax, no 5.1 kHz channel

scenes.narration: The exam asks about fax on the Thrane and Thrane F250 and F500, too. Their facsimile operation is configured as Group 3 fax via the 3.1 kilohertz audio channel, for analog fax applications. Group 3 is the standard for ordinary analog fax machines, the kind that send a page as sound over a phone line. The traps change one detail. Group 3 via the standard voice channel would garble the tones. Group 3 via the ISDN channel uses the wrong port. And there's no Group 5 fax and no 5.1 kilohertz channel at all.

params.title: The SIM: the terminal's identity
items: SIM: Subscriber Identity Module
An integrated circuit device
Securely stores the Inmarsat identity and an authentication key
The network uses them to verify the terminal

onScreen: Stores the Inmarsat identity and authentication key
scenes.narration: Whatever plugs into it, the terminal itself must first be accepted by the network. How does the network know which terminal is calling, and that it's genuine? Like a mobile phone, every Fleet Broadband terminal holds a SIM, a Subscriber Identity Module. It's an integrated circuit device, a small card carrying a chip, that securely stores the Inmarsat identity and an authentication key. The identity says who the terminal is. The authentication key is a secret code that proves it, like a key that fits only one lock. The network uses them to verify the terminal before it allows calls or data. The other choices describe something else: rights management, high-speed data features, or a read and write data device.

blocks.label: Enter the PUK
blocks.note: PIN Unlock Key, from the airtime provider

scenes.narration: The SIM is protected by a PIN, a Personal Identification Number, much like a bank card. Enter the wrong PIN too many times and the SIM card locks itself, so nobody can keep guessing. To unlock the SIM card in a Fleet Broadband terminal, you use the PUK, which stands for PIN Unlock Key. The airtime provider, the company that sells the satellite service, supplies it. The wrong choices use the PUK for credit card calls, telephone extensions or long distance blocks. It has one job: unlocking the SIM, after which you can set a new PIN.

params.title: Standard IP or Streaming?
rows: Time critical uses, like live video

onScreen: Streaming: time critical, like live video
scenes.narration: Once the SIM is accepted, the terminal can carry data. As a BGAN service, Fleet Broadband offers 2 kinds of data connection. Think of a road. Standard IP is the shared road: everyone in the area uses the same capacity, and you get whatever share is free. That's fine for ordinary e-mail, file transfer and Internet traffic, which can wait a moment. Inmarsat BGAN Streaming Data service is like a reserved lane: an exclusive, high-priority connection, ideal for time critical applications such as live video, which stutters if its data arrives late. So for Streaming, choose the exclusive, high-priority connection, not the e-mail and Internet service, the web interface or ISDN.

blocks.label: Just pressing DISTRESS
blocks.note: Sends a real alert at once

blocks.label: Test Distress Alarm sent
blocks.note: Expected and handled as a test

onScreen: Pressing DISTRESS sends a real alert to an RCC
LES arranges the test in advance
scenes.narration: One last feature, and the most serious: distress. Inmarsat terminals have a DISTRESS button under a cover. Press it, and a real distress alert goes straight to an RCC, a Rescue Coordination Centre: the shore center that organizes searches and rescues. So how do you test the Inmarsat Distress Alarm without starting a rescue? Use service number 33, the technical assistance code, to arrange a Distress Alarm test transmission with the LES in advance. The test alert is then expected, and handled as a test. Don't just lift the cover and press the button. Telling the Coast Guard first, or sending a safety call just before, doesn't make it a test either. Only the arrangement with the LES does.

params.title: A serial data link: DTE and DCE

blocks.label: EIA-232 cable
blocks.note: Sends data 1 bit at a time

onScreen: EIA-232 cable, 1 bit at a time
Inmarsat-C data port wired as DCE
scenes.narration: You now know how each system should work, and that's exactly what troubleshooting needs: the trick is to ask what each symptom rules out. We'll start with a computer that won't talk to an Inmarsat-C terminal. The terminal's data port connects to a computer or printer through an EIA-232 cable, an older standard that sends data 1 bit at a time. The computer or printer is DTE, data terminal equipment. The Inmarsat-C data port is wired as DCE, data communications equipment. Each end transmits on one wire and listens on another, and DCE and DTE are wired opposite to each other. So a plain straight-through cable lines up one end's transmit with the other end's receive.

blocks.label: Straight-through EIA-232 cable
blocks.note: Stop bits and parity just match

onScreen: Stop bits and parity just need to match
Null modem cable crosses transmit and receive
scenes.narration: That's the working setup, with a straight-through cable. Data flows as long as the stop bit and parity settings match at both ends. A stop bit marks the end of each character, and parity is a simple error check. They're ordinary settings; they don't block the link. So what would prevent communication between the data port and the DTE? Using a null modem cable to connect the DTE. A null modem cable crosses the transmit and receive lines inside it, for joining 2 devices wired the same way, such as 2 computers. Put it between the DCE data port and the DTE, and the crossing undoes the match: transmit meets transmit, receive meets receive, and neither end hears the other.

params.title: Inmarsat-C: test flag and ACB
rows: Test flag set in a Distress Alert
A TEST alert: no rescue response starts
A message couldn't be delivered: here's why
Access to the Inmarsat system barred

onScreen: Test flag set: a TEST alert
NDN: a message could not be delivered
ACB on an NDN: access barred
scenes.narration: Once the link works, the terminal reports back with messages and codes. Start with 2 from Inmarsat-C. Remember the distress test? How can an LES or RCC tell an Inmarsat-C Distress Alert is a TEST transmission? A flag in the message, a marker set inside the alert, identifies it as a test alert. So it's recognized at once and no rescue response starts; staff don't have to verify each alert by hand. When a message can't be delivered, the system sends back an NDN, a Non-Delivery Notification, with a failure code. The code ACB means access to the Inmarsat system has been barred: the network has blocked that terminal or service. It isn't an answer-back, bit error or channel failure.

params.title: Fleet 77 messages and codes
rows: The RX2 to ACU link has failed
RX2 locked on the NCSC, valid frame
Not registered to the MPDS network

onScreen: RX2 or ACU Comm error: RX2 to ACU link failure
Locked on the NCSC, valid frame: normal
scenes.narration: 2 more codes come from the older Fleet 77 terminal. Inside it, a second receiver, RX2, exchanges data with the Antenna Control Unit, the ACU. If that link fails, the terminal displays RX2 Comm error or ACU Comm error; Comm is short for communication. RX2 locking onto the NCSC, the NCS common channel from earlier, or receiving a valid frame, a complete block of data, are signs of normal operation. Then there's MPDS, the Mobile Packet Data Service, which sends data in small chunks called packets. If a connection to the MPDS network fails, the terminal shows zero zero F zero H or zero zero F one H: it is not registered to the MPDS network. Codes starting 77 are traps.

onScreen: Not EPIRBs, SARTs or survival craft radios
scenes.narration: Some faults come from outside the equipment. Transmitters operating in the 3 to 30 megahertz range, the HF band ships use for long-range radio, can interfere with Fleet 77 and Fleet 55 systems, and so can shipboard radars in close proximity. Both are powerful and close by. A nearby HF transmitter induces strong RF currents in the antenna cables, meaning it creates them without touching, and a radar beam sweeping across the antenna can overload its sensitive receiver. The exam also offers EPIRBs, Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacons, SARTs, Search And Rescue Radar Transponders, and survival craft radios. Those are low power and seldom transmit, so they aren't the likely source.

callouts.label: Ferrite clamps on the coax cable
They suppress HF induced on the outside of the shield
The L-band signal inside passes untouched
A longer ground lead would make it worse
Not a low-pass filter: it would block the L-band signal

onScreen: Suppress induced HF on the shield
scenes.narration: And the cure? To resolve interference induced from nearby HF transmitters, install ferrite clamps on the coax cable to suppress induced RF. Ferrite is a magnetic ceramic material, and a clamp snaps around the cable like a thick bead. The unwanted HF energy rides on the outside of the coax shield, and the ferrite chokes it off there, without affecting the L-band signal travelling inside the cable. A longer ground lead would make it worse, since a longer wire picks up more HF, like a bigger antenna. And a low-pass filter, which passes low frequencies and blocks high ones, would block the L-band signal and let the HF through: exactly backwards.

blocks.label: Antenna power fuse in the ADE
LNA
blocks.note: Gets no power, passes no signal

onScreen: DC travels up the coax center conductor
No voltage on the center pin
Blown antenna power fuse in the ADE
A bad LNA would leave the voltage
scenes.narration: Back inside the system, here are 3 Inmarsat-C antenna faults. First, a refresher: the LNA up at the antenna needs power. The terminal sends it DC, direct current, a steady one-way flow like a battery's, up the same coax that brings the signal down, on its center conductor, which ends at the antenna's center pin. Suppose the terminal shows a No Receive Signal alarm, and there's no voltage on the antenna center pin. The most likely cause is a blown antenna power fuse in the ADE, the above deck equipment. The supply path is open, so the LNA gets no power and passes no signal. A defective LNA is the trap: it would still leave the voltage on the pin.

params.title: Won't LOG IN: the swap test

blocks.label: Install a replacement ADE
blocks.note: The original ADE is at fault

onScreen: Test cable and new ADE in view of the satellite
scenes.narration: Second fault: the Inmarsat-C terminal will not LOG IN, meaning it can't sign on to the network. To narrow it down, connect a test antenna cable with a new ADE, placed in view of the satellite. If the terminal now logs in, the terminal below deck is proven good, and so is the satellite, so trying a different satellite with the original ADE wouldn't help. The fault is in the original ADE: install a replacement ADE. Replacing the AZ or EL motor is a trap too. AZ is azimuth, the compass direction an antenna faces, and EL is elevation, its angle up from the horizon. Inmarsat-C antennas are fixed omni-directional units with no AZ or EL motors to replace.

callouts.label: Set the meter to measure resistance, in ohms
Short one end of the coax: center conductor to shield
Measure at the other end: a good cable reads almost 0 ohms
Above 1 ohm: replace the cable

onScreen: Short one end of the coax
Measure at the other end: almost 0 ohms is good
scenes.narration: Third fault: the terminal will not LOG IN and shows an Antenna not connected alarm. That points to the coax. Test it with an ohmmeter: the resistance setting of a multimeter, the technician's meter for voltage, current and resistance. Resistance is how strongly a path opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms. Short one end of the coax, joining its center conductor to its shield. Then measure between them at the other end. Current now runs up the center and back along the shield, so you test the whole loop. A good cable reads almost 0 ohms. Above 1 ohm, a conductor or connector is damaged: replace the cable. Changing satellites or replacing the antenna won't fix a broken cable.

params.title: How a tracking antenna finds the satellite

callouts.label: AZ motor turns the antenna around: azimuth
EL motor tilts it up and down: elevation
Level platform sensor: the horizontal reference
Antenna control module: finds the signal and locks on

onScreen: Antenna control module: finds and locks on
scenes.narration: Inmarsat-C's antenna is fixed. Stabilized tracking antennas, like Fleet Broadband's, have moving parts, and faults to match. When one starts up, it initializes: it searches the sky, finds the satellite and locks on. 4 parts share the work. The AZ motor turns the antenna around in azimuth, and the EL motor tilts it up and down in elevation. The level platform sensor tells the controller which way is level, its horizontal reference, so it can measure elevation. And the antenna control module, part of the antenna-control electronics, steers the search, recognizes the satellite's signal and locks onto it. Knowing who does what lets you reason from a symptom to the faulty part.

params.title: Passes the satellite, won't initialize
items: Antenna goes past the satellite's AZ EL, won't initialize
Pointed by hand, it acquires the signal
Motors work, RF path works
Most likely: a faulty antenna control module

scenes.narration: Suppose the antenna goes past the AZ EL of the satellite, its azimuth and elevation, but does not initialize. Yet you can point it at the satellite by hand and acquire the signal. What's left? The motors clearly work, since the antenna swept right past the satellite. The coax and the RF path clearly work too, since manual pointing gets a signal. So the most likely problem is a faulty antenna control module, the part that should have recognized the signal and locked on. A defective coax, or a bad IF, intermediate frequency, amplifier, a stage deeper inside the receiver, is ruled out by the signal you got by hand.

params.title: Up and down, or straight up?
rows: Creeps up and down after initialization
Up and down is elevation, not azimuth
Stiff when turned by hand: replace it
It should hold firmly between steps

onScreen: Creeps up and down: an elevation problem
Check the EL step motor with power off; stiff means replace
Points straight up and stops: level platform sensor
scenes.narration: 2 more symptoms, and here the direction of movement is the clue. If the antenna creeps up and down after initialization, that's an elevation problem, not azimuth, which would show as side-to-side movement. A step motor turns in small exact steps and should hold firmly between them. So check the EL step motor with the power off: turn it by hand, and if it's stiff, replace it. If instead the antenna tries to initialize, then points straight up and stops, the most likely problem is a defective level platform sensor. Without its horizontal reference, the controller can't work out elevation, so it drives to its straight-up limit and gives up. The motors are fine; they moved it.

params.title: Antenna keeps hunting: check the event log

callouts.label: Antenna continuously changes azimuth after initialization
Open the terminal's Web interface
Check the event log before replacing any parts

scenes.narration: Sometimes the antenna moves but never settles. Then the terminal itself can tell you why. If an Inmarsat Fleet Broadband antenna continuously changes azimuth after initialization, hunting from side to side, use the Web interface to check the event log. The Web interface is the terminal's set of built-in web pages, opened in a laptop's web browser. The event log is the terminal's record of faults and events, such as a lost heading input from the ship's compass, or a tracking fault. Checking it shows the cause before you replace any parts. Replacing a motor first is guesswork, and checking the EL motor looks at the wrong axis.

onScreen: AC present at the supply input
Component failure inside the power supply
scenes.narration: Next, an Inmarsat-C terminal that won't power up at all. Its power supply takes in the ship's AC, alternating current, the main electrical supply that reverses direction many times a second, and turns it into the steady DC the terminal's circuits need. If AC voltage is present at the input terminals of the power supply, power is reaching it, yet nothing comes out. So the cause is a component failure within the power supply itself, such as a blown fuse or a failed part inside it. A bad coax cable, a receiver stage or a monitor wouldn't stop the unit from switching on.

params.title: Laptop can't connect: the wrong socket

callouts.label: Ethernet cable plugged into the terminal's ISDN port
Same style RJ-45 connector as the LAN ports, so it fits
It carries ISDN, not Ethernet: no IP link
Fix: move the cable to a LAN port

onScreen: Same RJ-45 connector as the LAN ports
ISDN, not Ethernet: no IP link
Move it to a LAN port
scenes.narration: Now the technician's own laptop. There are 2 ways it can fail to connect with a Fleet Broadband terminal. The first is the wrong socket: the Ethernet cable is plugged into the terminal's ISDN port. That port has the same style RJ-45 connector as the LAN ports, RJ-45 being the plug used on network cables, so the cable fits. But the ISDN port carries ISDN signals, not Ethernet, so there's no IP link at all. Move the cable to a LAN port.

params.title: Laptop can't connect: the wrong address
rows: Can't find the terminal's web server

onScreen: Right IP address: reaches the terminal's web server
Wrong IP address: can't find it
scenes.narration: The second way is the wrong address. An IP address is the number that identifies a device on a network, like a house address, and a URL is the web address you type into a browser. To reach the terminal's settings pages, you type the terminal's IP address into the laptop's web browser as the URL, and the browser finds the terminal's built-in web server, the part of the terminal that serves those pages. Enter the wrong IP address, and the browser cannot find the terminal's built-in web server, even though the cable and the terminal are fine. Check the address and try again.

blocks.label: Standard IP channel
blocks.note: Throughput shared by all its users

onScreen: Channel busy with many active users
scenes.narration: Finally, a connection that works but crawls. A Fleet Broadband terminal's observed bit rate, the number of bits per second it actually gets, drops when a Standard IP satellite channel is busy with many active users. Remember the shared road. Standard IP throughput, the total data the channel can carry, is shared among everyone using it at the time. As more users join, each one's share shrinks, like traffic at rush hour, and the bit rate your terminal observes falls. Nothing is broken. An application that can't tolerate that needs the exclusive Streaming service instead. The trap choices blame protocols like FTP, but those ride on TCP IP anyway.

scenes.narration: Let's gather up the key facts. Inmarsat-C receives on 1530.0 to 1545.0 megahertz and transmits on the higher band, 1626.5 to 1645.5 megahertz. The low noise amplifier at the antenna sets the noise figure. Inmarsat-C carries text, never voice, through an RHC, omni-directional antenna. GPS uses 24 satellites in 6 planes at 20,200 kilometers and 55 degrees, needs at least 4 of them, and sends L1 on 1575.42 and L2 on 1227.60 megahertz. LRIT sends the GPS position over Inmarsat-C, an APR every 6 hours, 4 a day. On Fleet Broadband, fax uses 3.1 kilohertz audio, and distress tests are arranged through service number 33. And when troubleshooting, ask what each symptom rules out.
